title: Autonomous-System-Wide Unique BGP Identifier for BGP-4
summary: This standards-track document relaxes the BGP Identifier definition to a 4-octet unsigned non-zero integer and requires uniqueness only within an autonomous system. It does not change other BGP behavior.

eli5.summary: Each router in a network needs a name tag only unique inside its own team. This relaxes the old rule that it must be unique worldwide.

subtitle: BGP Identifiers become any non-zero 4-octet integer, unique only within an AS.

tldr.problem: BGP required the BGP Identifier to be a valid IPv4 host address and distinct between peers, which fails in cases such as an IPv6-only network.
tldr.mechanism: The identifier is redefined as a 4-octet, unsigned, non-zero integer needing uniqueness only within an AS, with OPEN error handling and collision resolution adjusted to match.
tldr.outcome: The RFC concludes this introduces no backward compatibility issues. It updates RFC 4271.

today: RFC 6286 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271. The metadata lists no later RFC replacing or updating it.

sections.title: The Problem with IPv4-Based Identifiers
sections.content:
In RFC 4271, the BGP Identifier is a valid IPv4 host address assigned to the speaker, and deployed code requires two speakers to have distinct identifiers to connect. That breaks down where no IPv4 address is available, such as an IPv6-only network.

RFC 6286 relaxes both rules. It updates RFC 4271.
sections.eli5: Routers used to need an old-style address as a name tag. This lets them use any number instead.

sections.title: The Relaxed Definition
sections.content:
The identifier is a 4-octet, unsigned, non-zero integer that should be unique within an AS. It is determined on startup and is the same for every local interface and every BGP peer.

For OPEN messages, the "Bad BGP Identifier" error subcode is used if the identifier is zero, or if it equals the local identifier and the message is from an internal peer.
sections.eli5: The tag is any non-zero number, picked once when the router starts, and it must not clash with teammates.

sections.title: Connection Collision Resolution
sections.content: Two external peers may now share an identifier. In that case, if the BGP Identifiers of the peers in a connection collision are identical, the connection initiated by the speaker with the larger AS number is preserved. This covers 4-octet AS numbers (RFC 4893).
sections.eli5: If two routers from different teams have the same tag and both call each other, the one from the team with the bigger number wins.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
An identifier allocated under RFC 4271 fits the revised definition. A BGP Confederation counts as one AS. A supporting speaker cannot share an identifier with an external neighbor until that neighbor is upgraded.

The RFC checks other uses of the identifier (the AGGREGATOR attribute, route reflection, route selection) and concludes there are no backward compatibility issues. It says there are no new security considerations.
sections.eli5: Old name tags still work, and the other places that use the tag keep working.

references.text: Rekhter, Y., Ed., Li, T., Ed., and S. Hares, Ed., "A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)", RFC 4271, January 2006.
Vohra, Q. and E. Chen, "BGP Support for Four-octet AS Number Space", RFC 4893, May 2007.
